tier_reason: First-party page (uppbox/uppweb/www.tpp/vsstd_en-us.tpp) carries the full benchmark code, GCC 4.1.3 and -O3, but the CPU is given only as 'Core 2 Duo, 2.7 Ghz' with no model number, the two input files (a 3.93 KB and a 58 KB .cpp file) are not identified, and how the standard-allocator runs were configured is not stated, so it is not reproducible enough for A; the in-repo rerun (benchmarks/idmapBench/info.txt, 2020) states neither hardware nor flags.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 2007 page (vsstd_en-us.tpp), best of std::map/tr1::unordered_map vs U++ VectorMap: 3.93 KB file, GCC64: std map 4.2 s, unordered_map 3.7 s, U++ 0.8 s (ratio U++/std 4.6); STL on the U++ heap 3.2 s / 3.0 s (ratio U++/STL 3.8). GCC32: 5.3 / 4.9 / 1.1 s, ratios 4.5 and 3.5. 58 KB file, GCC64: 55 / 43 / 8.8 s, ratios 4.9 and 3.9; GCC32: 70 / 56 / 11 s, ratios 5.1 and 4.1. Newer in-repo run of the updated benchmark (benchmarks/idmapBench/main.cpp with std::unordered_map, alice30.txt input, 1000 iterations; benchmarks/idmapBench/info.txt, 2020-08-30, CLANGx64 Blitz Release build on Windows, hardware and flags not stated, values printed as 'ms' but evidently a finer unit): on the U++ heap VectorMap 1365093 vs STL hash_map 3272627 and std::map 4835707 (about 2.4x vs the best STL container, derived from page data); with USEMALLOC (standard malloc for both) VectorMap 2260672 vs hash_map 4058483 (about 1.8x, derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.1.3 20070929 prerelease (Ubuntu 4.1.2-16ubuntu2) on Ubuntu 7.10 i386 and AMD64, -O3; benchmark defines NDEBUG; the page does not say how the standard-allocator runs were built (the current benchmark package uses the U++ USEMALLOC config flag). 2020 rerun: CLANGx64 Release (Blitz, full debug info), flags not listed.
corrections.hardware: Core 2 Duo, 2.7 GHz, 2GB RAM (no CPU model number given)
corrections.caveats: Benchmark is first-party and 2007-vintage (GCC 4.1.3, tr1::unordered_map, Core 2 Duo), and the repo's own 2020 rerun of the updated benchmark (benchmarks/idmapBench/info.txt, Clang x64 on Windows, std::unordered_map) shows the gap shrinking to about 2.4x on the U++ heap and about 1.8x with malloc for both, so the 4.5-5.1x headline is outdated. The measured ratio mixes four effects (container, String vs std::string, U++ FileIn::Get vs per-character std::ifstream::get, and the allocator), so it is not a container-only result; the page itself says the main reason for not using the standard library is not performance. Input files of the 2007 run are not identified (the default input is the benchmark's own main.cpp; the 58 KB file is unnamed), the CPU has no model number, and the allocator switch is not described, so the 2007 run cannot be reproduced exactly. Page only reports GCC rows although the code has an MSVC branch. The rendered ultimatepp.org page was not opened; the repo copy of the topic file was. Category is a judgement call: the benchmark is a word-index container test and fits hash-maps-sets (or allocators) better than filesystems-and-io.

notes: Numbers on the page match the record exactly, but tier A is not supported: CPU without model number, unnamed input files, unstated allocator configuration; downgraded to C. The repo's newer run (benchmarks/idmapBench/info.txt) shows only about 1.8-2.4x on Clang x64, which the orchestrator may want as the headline; category filesystems-and-io looks wrong (hash-maps-sets fits). Metadata confirmed: BSD-2-Clause, 994 stars, last commit 2026-10-07, not archived.

GPU (Tesla T4) vs one CPU thread, host/device transfers excluded.

corrections.license: Apache-2.0 (Thrust, with portions under BSL-1.0 and a FreeBSD-derived licence); CUB, which supplies thrust::sort's CUDA radix sort, is BSD-3-Clause; libcu++ is Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception
corrections.caveats: This compares a GPU radix sort (Thrust dispatching to CUB) with single-threaded std::sort on one vCPU, so it measures GPU vs one CPU core and excludes host/device transfers (std::copy and device_vector construction sit outside the timers); it is not a library-to-library win. The thrust::sort timing includes CUB's per-call temporary-storage cudaMalloc/cudaFree. The evidence is a student project README (Josh0323/Project2-Stream-Compaction, fork of the course template, 0 stars, no licence; one machine, host compiler and standard library not stated, CPU model only 'Xeon @ 2.30GHz', 16M full-range run missing because of a VM restart), so tier C. The Thrust project README and NVIDIA/cccl contain no performance numbers; a vendor claim that thrust::sort is '5x to 100x faster than STL and TBB' was seen only as a search-result snippet and is not used. Thrust development moved into NVIDIA/cccl (standalone NVIDIA/thrust archived 2024-03-21); last_commit and star counts for the live repo are from NVIDIA/cccl. Category changed from the guessed thread-pools-work-stealing because the only numeric comparison is a sort.

tier_reason: Third-party benchmark code is public (Red-Portal/thread-pool-benchmark: main.cpp, benchmark_candidates/cpp_threads/cpp_threads.cpp, benchmark_candidates/progschj_ThreadPool/progschj_ThreadPool.cpp) with compiler and CPU model stated, but its CMakeLists.txt never applies the -O3 flags and sets no build type, so the run was probably unoptimized (capped at C); single run, obscure 30-star suite.

corrections.caveats: Benchmark is a small third-party repo (Red-Portal/thread-pool-benchmark, 30 stars, archived 2022-06-10, GPL-3.0 benchmark code) with only two workloads and a single 'example results' run per row; its CMakeLists.txt builds a BUILD_FLAGS string with -std=c++14 -g -O3 but only prints it and never applies it, and no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE is set, so the times are probably from an unoptimized build. Baseline is std::async(std::launch::async) spawning one thread per task (1024 row tasks for the matrix multiplication), the weakest std::thread usage; ThreadPool (4 workers) wins by 3.7% on the fluid solver and loses by 15% on the matrix multiplication, and every other pool in the table (Sean Parent variants, GCD, TBB) beats it on both, so it is not shown to be faster. The ThreadPool repo has no benchmark or performance number of its own and was last committed on 2014-09-26 (no maintenance).

notes: Numbers match the Red-Portal README exactly (fluid 1567.72 vs 1628.18 ms, matmul 562.66 vs 488.52 ms); baseline really is std::async per task, and ThreadPool is mixed to slower against it, so record shortcomings 'not faster' and 'unoptimized build likely'. Metadata confirmed: Zlib, 8.8k stars, 2.3k forks, 28 commits, last commit 2014-09-26, not archived.
